Sketch, staying at the mechanism level (real fields, not guessed):

Our /review, called with sign=true, returns a verdict_proof carrying decision_ref = sha256(JCS({artifact_hash, artifact_type, policy_version, verdict, source_class})) plus a signature over that payload from our published key.

Binding into ConsultEscrow:

Your open Q — is the L4 sig a distinct, ecrecover-friendly signature we can also produce over decision_ref? Yes, and more: the on-chain-cheap leg is already live.

L4 is standard EIP-712 secp256k1. /verify recovers it with recoverTypedDataAddress, domain KYA-L4 (name/version/chainId/verifyingContract=registry), signer = the gateway attestor — so it’s already a distinct sig from the Nostr /ledger entry, the same pattern you’d reuse for decision_ref.
And ConsultEscrow.release(jobId, resultHash, sig) already recomputes commitmentHash = keccak256(abi.encode(jobId, resultHash)) on-chain and requires _recover(commitmentHash, sig) == job.attestor, where _recover is EIP-191 ecrecover. That’s the mainnet one you reviewed. So there’s no relayer to build on our side — the escrow already ecrecovers a secp256k1 attestor sig over a job-bound commitment.
So releaseAgainstVerdict maps almost 1:1 onto that. Two reuse paths, neither needs an off-chain relayer:

(A) /review emits a distinct secp256k1 sig over decision_ref — exactly how we emit the EIP-712 L4 alongside the Nostr /ledger. releaseAgainstVerdict reuses our _recover verbatim.
(B) keep the schnorr /ledger sig and verify it on-chain with the BIP340 verifier you already built for the ENS-recovery escrow (Nostr schnorr = BIP340 over secp256k1). No new signature type — reuses your code.
The actually-new piece isn’t the curve, it’s the second signer. release() today recovers to job.attestor (us, the gateway). Your verdict recovers to your published reviewer key — a different party. So the escrow has to trust that reviewer key: either named per-job in the Job struct the way attestor is now, or a small registered-reviewer set. That’s the real design decision.

On the three legs you laid out — agree on all of them:

record(digest) on the consult output → artifact_hash is the OCP-committed digest, provably about THIS output (same anti-substitution binding WYRIWE does for input-provenance). In our escrow that digest is resultHash, so your check (a) is just artifact_hash == the committed resultHash for jobId — one comparison.
/review(artifact_hash, artifact_type) → signed verdict_proof.
releaseAgainstVerdict checks (a) the hash binding, (b) verdict == pass → release to provider; fail → the deadline-refund path we already have.
Framing I’d push: don’t replace release(), compose it. release() proves “provider delivered this output.” releaseAgainstVerdict() adds “and an independent reviewer judged it pass.” Two-attestor — gateway completeness + independent policy verdict — is a stronger claim than either alone, and it’s the composition-note story made executable.

Happy to spec the Job-struct reviewer-key field + a releaseAgainstVerdict stub on our side once we pick (A) vs (B). I lean (A) for the demo timeline (pure reuse of our ecrecover path), (B) longer-term (keeps your signing native). Your call on which — worth a real conversation, agreed.

Quick one, in the spirit of the house — I found a seam in my own demo by recomputing, so I’m exposing it rather than quietly patching.

Wiring Damon’s amber-state item into /verify, I walked straight into the failure he’d named. My checker was binary — green or red — so when the L3 on-chain read couldn’t resolve, it rendered a could-not-check as a did-not-match. A red that wasn’t a real mismatch. Exactly the lie Damon said a checker must never tell, and Pavlo’s ternary door (valid / invalid / unverifiable) is the same truth one layer up: “unverifiable” is not a weak “invalid”, it’s a different state.

But the amber wasn’t even the root cause — it was masking a worse bug. The read was on the wrong chain. My L3 recipe read mainnet; the OCP record() anchor actually lives on Base Sepolia. The tx was real and green the whole time — my checker was just looking in the wrong place and calling the record a liar. Recompute caught what a screenshot never would.

Three fixes, all in the honest direction:

Ternary now. green = recomputed & matched · red = recomputed & didn’t · amber = couldn’t recompute (RPC/network), with retry. Amber is never a pass and never a fail.
Right chain + redundancy. L3 reads Base Sepolia across a fallback list of RPCs — one dead provider ambers, it doesn’t fail.
The good part — I stopped checking “does the anchor tx exist” and started recomputing the digest it actually wrote on-chain and binding it to keccak256(utf8(query)). Same anti-substitution binding WYRIWE does for input-provenance, and the same move your verdict-binding needs, Fede. Payoff: a tamper now cascades into the anchor too — edit one byte and Raw + Provenance + L4 + L3 all go red together, while Output stays green because I didn’t touch the output. The checker tells you exactly which link broke.
And the disclosure, plainly: the per-action attestation anchor is Base Sepolia, not mainnet. Identity (8004 registry) and settlement (ConsultEscrow) are mainnet; the high-frequency record() anchor is on Base because anchoring every action on L1 is silly. I’d been about to say “read straight from mainnet” on stage — that would’ve been wrong, so it’s now “read straight from the chain it was written to.” Multi-chain is the honest shape, not a thing to hide.

(B) it is — and I agree it’s the right call for the reason you gave, not just the timeline. Making you stand up and maintain a second signature type forever, to serve a mechanism that outlives the submission by years, is exactly the kind of surface area we shouldn’t add. Native schnorr on your side + your existing BIP340 verifier on-chain = proven code both ends, nothing new to trust.

The one thing that decides “cheap enough” is how your ENS-recovery verifier checks the sig. If it’s the ecrecover-trick — mapping BIP340 verification onto a single ecrecover call — it’s a few thousand gas and ConsultEscrow can call it inline without blinking. If it’s doing native EC ops on-chain (modexp / point math), that’s a different cost order and we’d want to actually measure before committing to inline verification vs a cheaper path. So: which is it? If it’s ecrecover-style, I think we’re already done on the gas question.

On the reviewer-key field — one detail so we spec it right: a BIP340 key is x-only, 32 bytes, not an ecrecover address. So it can’t be a mirror of the current attestor field (that’s an address, recovered via ecrecover in release()). The Job wants a separate bytes32 reviewerPubkey, and releaseAgainstVerdict calls bip340.verify(reviewerPubkey, decisionRef, sig) — a genuinely different verification method sitting next to the ecrecover one. Which is a nice statement in itself: completeness proven by ecrecover(attestor), soundness proven by BIP340(reviewer), same escrow.

Composition, not replacement: release() stays (provider delivered THIS output — ecrecover attestor over the job commitment). releaseAgainstVerdict(jobId, verdictProof) adds the second leg — (a) verdictProof.artifact_hash == the OCP digest committed for jobId, (b) verdict == pass, © bip340.verify(reviewerPubkey, decisionRef, sig). All three → release to provider; fail verdict → the deadline-refund path we already have.

Yes to speccing the Job struct together — say the word. Open question I’d want your read on: reviewerPubkey per-job at open() (named like attestor is now, caller commits to who reviews) vs a small registered-reviewer set the escrow trusts. Per-job is more flexible; a registered set is easier to reason about for a v1. Your call which we prototype.

Following up from the ConsultEscrow review — sharing something that might be worth the group's attention:

The pre-settlement layer. ConsultEscrow opens with a named provider — the consumer picks an agent first, then escrow locks the payment. That works perfectly for what it does. But upstream of escrow, there's a question the stack doesn't answer yet: when multiple agents can all handle the same task, how does the matching happen, and at what price? Escrow is the settlement leg; matching is the leg before it. Not a gap in ConsultEscrow itself, just a natural next piece of the puzzle.

There's already a draft ERC in this space. ERC-8195 — Task Market Protocol (TMP), by Beau Williams (Atlassian, Sydney). It defines five procurement modes, including an Auction mode (sealed-bid, lowest wins — similar to SP1's prover network model). Actor-agnostic (human / AI agent / IoT all treated uniformly), built on ERC-8004 identity. It's paired with his companion ERC-8194 (PGTR — keyless transaction authorization for lightweight participants).

Both are Draft (March 2026), and they compose naturally with the layers we already have:

ERC-8195 (TMP)     →  Task → Agent matching + auction  ← missing
ConsultEscrow       →  Pay-on-delivery custody           ← done
ERC-8275 Reputation →  Event-derived scoring             ← done

Why it's worth keeping an eye on. If TMP stabilizes, it'd be nice if the escrow layer and the matching layer compose cleanly — an auction winner on TMP should be able to flow into ConsultEscrow without glue code. Right now the interfaces are different shapes (createTask vs open), and that's fine for parallel drafts, but alignment early is easier than alignment later.

A few gentle next steps to consider together:

1. Worth a read — the Auction mode state machine in TMP (ethereum/ERCs PR #1604) maps to SP1's "bid → lowest wins → locked → submit → settle" pattern pretty cleanly.

Something like "we have a settlement layer here, here's how auction winners would flow through it, we'd love to make sure the interfaces compose well." The spec is still soft, now's the time.
3. If and when the group feels TMP is the right pre-settlement layer, we can add its interfaces to agent-ercs and make the composition explicit. No rush — just flagging it while the window for input is open.

Small update from the consultation-flow / A2A side — two things that land right where we’ve been circling on reputation.

1. Closing the loop is now perceivable, and recomputable at settlement.
The escrow already releases on delivery — attestor signs keccak256(abi.encode(jobId, resultHash)), the contract recomputes it and checks the attestor sig, so the payout is bound to that exact jobId (not replayable). What was missing was consumer-side legibility: you paid, the agent delivered, but nothing said “settled.” Added a settlement card that surfaces the release — amount out, the release() tx — and the part I like: it recomputes keccak256(utf8 resultText) == resultHash in the caller’s own browser, so the payment is provably bound to the exact delivered artifact. Don’t-trust-recompute applied to the money, not just the action. The SettlementProofRef it reads is the ERC-8275 OutcomeAttestation shape (verifierKey / settlementRef / verdictHash / result / publishesLosses).

2. Reputation, derived only from settlement outcomes we can all recompute.
Rather than a score you have to trust, derive it purely from ConsultEscrow events:

successful = Opened → Released
unsuccessful = Opened → Refunded
stale = Opened, window expired, unresolved
Score = a Wilson lower-bound (or Bayesian-smoothed) rate over those three, so small samples don’t outrank real track records and a single actor can’t farm a 1/1 — raw counts shown alongside so it’s fully re-derivable from chain. Because the deadline-refund makes losses structurally published (publishesLosses: true), the “unsuccessful” and “stale” buckets aren’t hideable — the reputation has to account for the misses. That’s the point: reputation as a recompute artifact, slotting into the ERC-8004 reputation axis + Fede’s operator-diversity seam under ERC-8275.

Not proposing a new leg — just noting the settlement + reputation surfaces are now concrete and demoable, and they compose cleanly with the consultation-flow note. Curious whether the successful / unsuccessful / stale trichotomy + the publishes-losses framing lines up with how you’d want the reputation section of the note to read.

Both pieces land right, and the trichotomy specifically is the right shape -- stale as its own bucket (not lumped into unsuccessful) matters because an unresolved timeout and an active refund are genuinely different signals, and publishesLosses:true means neither can be quietly dropped. Wilson lower-bound over that is the correct instinct for small-n reputation -- raw win-rate lets a lucky 1/1 outrank a real track record, the bound structurally can't. Raw counts alongside for re-derivability is exactly the doctrine, not decoration.

One real question, from a lesson Sarkar just pushed me through hard on the reputation_axis side: does the Wilson bound treat stale the same as unsuccessful in the underlying trial count, or does it weight/exclude them differently? They're not the same failure mode -- unsuccessful is a resolved dispute, stale is 'nobody ever confirmed either way.' If both feed the same bernoulli trial as equally-negative, a counterparty who's mostly ghosted (never actually delivered OR got refunded, just expired) reads identically to one who's genuinely disputed and lost -- worth naming explicitly in the note if it doesn't already, same 'does it gate the arithmetic or just annotate it' precision that mattered on our side. Settlement-card recompute (keccak256 of the delivered text, done in the caller's own browser) is the right move too -- don't-trust-recompute on the money leg closes a gap our own WYRIWE framing left open (we commit the input, you're closing the loop on the payout binding to the exact output).

This lands, and the trichotomy is the right shape — successful / unsuccessful / stale is the ternary verdict lifted to the history layer: "stale" is could-not-evaluate, and you kept it as its own bucket instead of folding it into failure. That's the part most reputation systems get wrong.
The bigger thing you did right: the score is derived, not asserted. Wilson bound over recomputable events with raw counts shown alongside means anyone can re-derive it from chain and disagree with your smoothing without disagreeing with your facts. That's reputation as a recompute artifact — score downstream of a gate, never inside it.

chronicle_checkpoint.v0 landed — the fourth Chronicle artifact.
Why it exists: collections are sets. collection_root is computed over sorted refs, which was deliberate — same set, any input order, same root — but the consequence is that arrival order is preserved nowhere. So the model couldn't express "history as of moment T", which means a write couldn't carry the committed view it was decided against. A checkpoint is that view, made addressable: entry_refs at the snapshot, prev_checkpoint, explicit sequence, own root.
Entry, collection and portfolio are untouched — no new fields, no changed derivation, all four existing golden vectors still pass byte-for-byte.
Two things worth flagging beyond the artifact itself:
verify no longer normalizes its input. It used to recompute the root over sorted refs, which meant an artifact stored with unsorted refs verified ok: true — the checker was silently fixing the thing it was checking. Same defect class as the ACE permutation vector, but in code rather than in a fixture. Checkpoint verification now recomputes over refs exactly as stored and separately asserts canonical order.
The sort comparator matters. localeCompare is ICU collation — locale- and ICU-version dependent — so Rust codepoint ordering, Python sorted() and a browser under a different locale can produce different orders for non-ASCII refs, hence different roots. Checkpoint sorts by codepoint. Same family as the uint64 sentinel and Infinity: a layer that isn't obliged to preserve something quietly doesn't.
Docs also now state the verification scope explicitly: verify* answers whether recomputation over stored canonical content yields the stored root, and nothing else. Shape validation lives at construction; consumers MUST validate shape before interpreting a verify result. Deferred to v1, deliberately: a malformed value isn't an invalid artifact, it isn't an instance of the type at all — reporting it as ok: false would collapse a shape state into a validity state, so it wants a distinct malformed outcome across all Chronicle verifiers rather than one patched boolean.
Golden vectors in chronicle-root-golden-vectors.json under checkpoint, generated by execution. Recompute rather than trust.

I have a framing question I’d like to share. In my view, truly trustless AI Agent applications require the outputs of agents to be committed onchain. The framing I'd push back on slightly: "work happens off-chain, chain only handles payments" treats settlement as the chain's only job. But payment is just the most obvious thing you can make non-repudiable — it isn't the interesting one.
What the chain is actually good for here is being the place a claim can't be quietly rewritten. That gives you four surfaces beyond payment, and we've been building on all of them this month:
Commitment — the digest of what an agent did, published where the agent's operator can't edit it afterwards. Off-chain work, on-chain irreversibility about what that work was.
Authorization — what the agent was permitted to do, evaluated at the position of the action rather than at the moment someone checks. That's ACE.
Verdicts — a review outcome bound to a specific artifact, so a settlement is tied to this output and not "a job was done".
History — the part that's still mostly missing across the ERC family: entries exist, but nobody standardized the admission rule that turns entries into a defensible track record.
Every one of those is worthless if the record is only as good as the operator's word — which is why the useful test for any of these use cases is: can a skeptic re-derive the claim without trusting whoever produced it? A task marketplace where payment settles on-chain but the work is unverifiable is exactly the "partial value" you're describing. The same marketplace where the deliverable's digest, the entitlement, and the verdict all recompute is a different product.
Real example, live: Merlini's /verify — a real mainnet agent action where all five checks re-derive in the skeptic's own browser, and tampering one byte of the input turns four rows red while the output stays green.

Sharp four-way split, Pavlo, and Verdicts is worth pushing on directly since it's the surface we build live: /review issues a signed, independently-recomputable verdict bound to artifact_hash before an action executes, published to a public /ledger so a skeptic re-derives it the same way as your five-check example, no trust in the operator's word required.

The distinction I'd add: Verdicts split into two real subclasses depending on WHEN the check runs, not just whether it's recomputable. Pre-action judgment (ours) issues before the irreversible step, so it can actually change the outcome. Post-hoc reconstruction (sounds like Merlini's /verify example, checking a mainnet action's inputs after the fact) proves what already happened was correct -- genuinely useful for audit, but structurally can't stop a bad action, only document it cleanly. Both recompute from public inputs and neither trusts the operator, but only one sits in the causal chain before the mistake.

On Jimmy's premise -- onchain commitment gets you non-repudiability, but it's not the only route. A signed proof anchored to a published key gives off-chain outputs the same 'can't be quietly rewritten' property without a gas cost or scalability ceiling. That's live today on our side: verdicts publish as signed Nostr events against a stable pubkey, no chain write needed to make the claim checkable.

The pre-action / post-hoc split is the right cut, and I'd take it further: they're not two grades of the same thing, they have different failure modes and you need both. A pre-action verdict can be wrong — it judges on inputs, before the world responds — and its failure is a bad decision made confidently. A post-hoc reconstruction can't be wrong about what happened, but its failure is being right too late. Neither replaces the other; a system with only pre-action verdicts has no way to discover its judgments were miscalibrated, and one with only post-hoc has no way to act on that.
The thing they share is that both must be minted against a position and never re-derived against "now" — which is the same discipline in both directions.
On anchoring: agreed that a chain write isn't the only route, and signed-against-a-stable-pubkey does buy the property. One boundary worth naming though. A signature gives non-repudiation — the author can't deny issuing this verdict. It doesn't give non-suppression — a relay can decline to serve an event, an operator can decline to publish the inconvenient verdict at all, and from the outside that's indistinguishable from "nothing happened". Chain ordering is expensive precisely because it buys a third party's view of completeness, not just authenticity.
Same shape as proof-of-outcome vs proof-of-control: the signature proves the verdicts you can see are real, and says nothing about the ones you can't. Which is fine if it's declared — a ledger that says "these are the verdicts the issuer chose to publish" is honest; one that implies "these are all of them" isn't. Worth stating which one /ledger claims to be, since a consumer's threat model differs a lot between them.

Rather than a list, the filter I'd use — a scenario is a real fit only if the party who benefits from the claim is not the party who can check it. Where those are the same person, verifiability is a nice-to-have. Where they diverge, it's the product.
Three sharpenings of that, in rough order of how ready they are:
Delegated spend. Someone gives an agent authority over money or assets and isn't watching. The question isn't "did the agent do well" but "did it act within what it was permitted, and can I show that to a third party later" — an auditor, a partner, a regulator. This is the one that's already technically ready: entitlement at action time, recomputable, no trust in the operator.
Agent-to-agent procurement. Agent A hires agent B, and neither operator has any reason to trust the other's logs. Reputation from signed self-reports collapses here — you need outcomes that recompute from settlement facts. That's exactly what's being built in this group, and the honest caveat is that it needs volume to be interesting: a track record of three jobs isn't a track record.
Compliance where the claim outlives the relationship. Anything where someone will ask "prove what your system did in March" long after the vendor, the model version, and the staff have changed. This is where portable evidence beats a vendor dashboard by a wide margin, because the dashboard is gone and the receipt still recomputes.
The scenario I'd be most careful with is anything where the underlying judgment is inherently subjective — creative work, advisory quality, "was this analysis good". You can make the record of the judgment recomputable, but that doesn't make the judgment right, and a system that blurs the two ends up laundering opinion through cryptography. Verifiable execution is a strong claim about process and a very weak one about taste.
Practical test for any candidate: name the skeptic. If you can't say who would want to check and why they'd doubt, the verifiability isn't load-bearing yet — and the honest answer might be that a database is fine for that use case.

Precise cut, and worth answering directly rather than hand-waving: /ledger claims neither. It's honest about being 'the verdicts we chose to publish,' not 'all of them' -- but until just now that honesty was implicit (nowhere stated, nowhere checkable), which is exactly the gap you're naming.

But I think the reduction loses the thing the primitive was for. Periodic co-signing gives no-rewriting: the tape only grew, history wasn't rewritten, prev chains cleanly. That's real and worth having. It does not give no-omission: a verdict that was computed and simply never written to the tape passes that check perfectly. The chain is clean, the sequence is monotonic, everything's green — because the witness only ever sees what made it into the tape, and omission happens upstream of the tape.
Those are two different properties, and only one of them is what suppression is about. An operator who dislikes a verdict doesn't rewrite history — that's detectable and dumb. They just don't write it in the first place.
Which is why the witness has to sit at compute-time rather than on a periodic sweep: not the same witness on a different schedule, a different position in the causal chain. Something has to observe that a verdict computation began for job X, before anyone knows the answer. Then a suppressed verdict is a computation with no corresponding entry — visible as a gap rather than as nothing at all.
So I'd say both, not either: checkpoints over the tape for no-rewriting (which is buildable today, exactly as you describe, and I'd take that build), plus an issuance-time counter for no-omission (which isn't, and is the part that actually needs specifying). That's a small, well-defined piece of work and it's mine to do.

Yes on the first — structured step outputs, not raw inference tokens. And the reason matters: raw sampling isn't reproducible, so hashing it as a predicate is meaningless. You can commit to it as evidence ("this is what came back"), but you can't require it to re-derive. The moment a recipe demands byte-equality on a model's raw output, it's guaranteed to fail for reasons that have nothing to do with tampering.
The second question is the harder one and I'd rather answer it plainly than talk around it: nothing in this stack proves a step actually went through the claimed model or MCP. Not ours, not anyone's here. What recomputation proves is that the record of the call wasn't rewritten — inputs commit, outputs commit, the binding between them holds, the declared parameters are fixed. It says nothing about whether the operator really called GPT-whatever or a cheaper model and wrote down the expensive one.
That's the boundary I'd draw explicitly: the receipt gates the record, not the world. An issuer who lies in the evidence from the start produces a receipt that recomputes perfectly — garbage in, admissible garbage out. Defenses against fabricated evidence live outside the receipt, and there are exactly three:
Hardware — attested execution, where the operator can't substitute. Real, but you've traded trusting the operator for trusting a chip vendor's attestation chain.
Provider signatures — if inference APIs signed their responses against a published key, this would collapse to a solved problem. They don't, and that's the single biggest missing piece in this whole space. Worth noticing that it's a business decision, not a technical limit.
Economics — the operator posts a bond, anyone can challenge with contradicting evidence, a successful challenge slashes. Doesn't make lying impossible, makes it expensive and non-repudiable after the fact.
Third one is the only one available today without new dependencies, and it's stake, not truth again — you're not proving honesty, you're pricing dishonesty and making it attributable.
The practical version: commit the input before the call, commit the output after, bind both to the declared model/version/parameters, and be honest in the artifact that the binding is attested rather than proven. A record that says "operator asserts this came from model X, and here's the signature they can't take back" is genuinely useful. One that implies the model attribution was verified is the exact overclaim this group keeps catching in other people's designs.

ERC-8301 is a good fit for one regime, but I would not call it a general no-omission solution.

The useful property is that run() and NewAgentTask mint an external workflow position before the result is known. If every required stage is contract-emitted, then a missing reply or missing transition becomes observable against that declared FSM. In that sense, ERC-8301 can serve as the issuance-time witness for workflow-anchored or settlement-anchored cases.

But the current draft does not define onAgentStep; it defines run → NewAgentTask → onAgentReply → onAgentProve. More importantly, it only sees steps that are actually routed through the contract. An operator can still perform or suppress an internal model/MCP step without submitting it, and the contract cannot detect what never entered its state machine.

There is also a narrower discoverability issue: the finalTaskHash traversal proves the selected execution path, not necessarily every attempted reply. Silent gate outcomes and losing competitive replies may be stored but excluded from the downstream prevReplyHashes chain, and the base interface currently has no standard event exposing every anchored reply.

So I would frame it as:

ERC-8301 provides no-rewriting and omission detectability for declared onchain workflow positions.

It does not prove that every internal agent step was declared, executed, or attributed to the claimed model/provider.

For a real no-omission profile, I think it would need:
- an event for every stored reply before gate selection;
- a monotonic per-run attempt/step sequence;
- declared timeout or expected-transition semantics;
- a distinct missing/unresolved state, not invalid;
- an explicit statement that model/MCP attribution remains attested unless independently proven.

That would make it compose cleanly with as_of checkpoints without overstating what the workflow contract can see.

I agree with the two-axis separation, but I would tighten two implementation claims.

A static FSM prevents an operator from routing around a hardcoded node, but it does not by itself force liveness. An operator may still decline to call the next transition or submit the transaction. What the static contract gives is a declared expected path; omission becomes detectable only when the implementation also defines expected-transition or timeout semantics. Otherwise “the step was suppressed” and “the workflow has not advanced yet” remain the same observation.

The second correction is more important: fixing the declared model, inputs, temperature, and other parameters does not guarantee byte-identical output from a hosted model. Provider routing, model revisions, numerical execution, batching, tool state, and external dependencies may still vary. Even temperature zero is not a general reproducibility guarantee.

So I would describe Scenario B as pinned or declared execution configuration, not deterministic execution, unless the implementation also pins the exact weights/runtime, decoding procedure, seed, all external inputs, and a reproducible execution environment.

The axes then remain clean:

- static vs dynamic FSM: whether required workflow positions are declared and omission can be detected;
- recomputable vs attested execution: whether the output can independently re-derive or only carries an attributable claim about how it was produced;
- judgment/verdict: whether the produced output satisfies the required predicate.

A static FSM proves that an owed step existed and, with timeout semantics, whether it completed. It still does not prove that the claimed model produced the output or that the output was correct.
